quests.question: The firm employs two hundred people, most of ___ work remotely.
quests.hint: The clause needs a relative pronoun right after 'of.' Which one follows a preposition when the antecedent is a group of people?
quests.explanation: 'Most of whom' combines a quantifier, a preposition, and a relative pronoun; after 'of,' a person takes 'whom.' 'Most of who' is impossible, and 'most of them' would join two full sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.
quests.correctAnswer: whom

quests.question: The museum owns three thousand paintings, several of ___ have never been exhibited.
quests.hint: The antecedent is a group of things, and the pronoun follows the preposition 'of.'
quests.explanation: Paintings are things, so the pronoun after 'of' is 'which': 'several of which.' 'That' cannot follow a preposition, 'whom' is for people, and 'them' would create a comma splice.
quests.correctAnswer: which

quests.question: The conference welcomed five hundred delegates, many of whom travelled from abroad. What does 'many of whom' refer to?
quests.hint: 'Whom' points back to the group named just before the comma. Ask who 'many' is a portion of.
quests.explanation: 'Many of whom' picks out part of the group 'five hundred delegates' and adds extra information about them. The conference itself is not a group of people, so 'whom' cannot refer to it.
quests.correctAnswer: the five hundred delegates

quests.question: The library holds thousands of books, only one of which ___ available online.
quests.hint: The verb follows the quantifier - 'one' - not the plural noun 'books.'
quests.explanation: In 'one of which,' the subject of the verb is 'one,' which is singular, so 'is' is correct. 'Are' is the common trap: it agrees with 'books,' but 'books' is inside the prepositional phrase 'of which.'
quests.correctAnswer: is
quests.grammarRule: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses

quests.question: Ten students applied, three of whom ___ offered scholarships.
quests.hint: Decide which word is the subject of the verb - 'three' or 'whom' - and whether the sentence is set in the past.
quests.explanation: The subject is 'three,' which is plural, and the story is told in the past, so 'were' is correct. 'Was' would suit 'one of whom,' and 'is' or 'has been' would shift the tense.
quests.correctAnswer: were
quests.grammarRule: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses

quests.question: The team lost five players, each of whom ___ replaced within a week.
quests.hint: 'Each' is singular, even though it refers to several players.
quests.explanation: 'Each' is grammatically singular, so the verb is 'was.' The plural noun 'players' sits inside 'of whom' and does not control the verb, so 'were' is the tempting mistake.
quests.correctAnswer: was
quests.grammarRule: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses

quests.question: Which sentence has the correct punctuation?
quests.hint: Quantifier clauses add extra information about a group already named, so they are set off from the main clause.
quests.explanation: A clause like 'most of whom had no experience' is non-defining, so it follows a comma; it has no comma after 'whom,' and it cannot use 'that.' Without the comma the clause is not properly separated, and extra commas break the phrase.
options: We interviewed twelve applicants, most of whom, had no experience.
We interviewed twelve applicants most of whom had no experience.
We interviewed twelve applicants, most of that had no experience.
We interviewed twelve applicants, most of whom had no experience.
quests.correctAnswer: We interviewed twelve applicants, most of whom had no experience.

quests.question: Which sentence is ungrammatical?
quests.hint: Three of these are acceptable ways to say the same thing. One joins two full clauses with nothing but a comma.
quests.explanation: 'All of them are safe' is a complete clause, so joining it to the first clause with only a comma is a comma splice. Using 'all of which,' adding 'and,' or splitting into two sentences all fix the problem.
options: The city has ten districts, and all of them are safe.
All ten districts of the city are safe.
The city has ten districts, all of which are safe.
The city has ten districts, all of them are safe.
quests.correctAnswer: The city has ten districts, all of them are safe.

quests.question: Why can't 'most of who' or 'most of that' replace 'most of whom' in 'The staff, most of whom are volunteers, run the shop'?
quests.hint: Think about which relative pronouns may follow a preposition such as 'of.'
quests.explanation: After a preposition, a relative pronoun for people must be 'whom'; 'who' and 'that' cannot follow a preposition at all. The rule has nothing to do with commas or with groups.
options: 'Who' and 'that' cannot refer to groups of people.
After a preposition, a relative pronoun for people must be 'whom,' and 'that' can never follow a preposition.
Quantifiers can only be used with 'which.'
quests.correctAnswer: After a preposition, a relative pronoun for people must be 'whom,' and 'that' can never follow a preposition.

quests.question: The committee, at ___ request the report was revised, has now approved it.
quests.hint: Look at the noun after the gap - 'request.' Who or what owns that request?
quests.explanation: 'At whose request' means 'at the committee's request,' so the possessive 'whose' is needed. This fronted-preposition-plus-'whose' pattern is common in formal writing, as in 'on whose behalf' and 'in whose honour.'
quests.correctAnswer: whose

quests.question: The charity, ___ behalf the funds were raised, thanked its donors.
quests.hint: The fixed phrase is 'on behalf of' someone. Which pronoun supplies the owner of the behalf?
quests.explanation: 'On whose behalf' = 'on the charity's behalf.' Possession requires 'whose'; 'on whom behalf' and 'on which behalf' cannot show ownership, and 'whose on' reverses the order.
quests.correctAnswer: on whose

quests.question: Which sentence uses the formal pattern correctly?
quests.hint: Two things must be right at once: the possessive pronoun and its position after the preposition.
quests.explanation: 'On whose recommendation' = 'on the manager's recommendation.' 'Who's' is a contraction of 'who is,' 'whom' cannot show possession, and 'whose on' puts the preposition in the wrong place.
options: The manager whose on recommendation we hired her has retired.
The manager on whom recommendation we hired her has retired.
The manager on whose recommendation we hired her has retired.
The manager on who's recommendation we hired her has retired.
quests.correctAnswer: The manager on whose recommendation we hired her has retired.

quests.question: Which version is standard and natural?
quests.hint: 'Look up to' means 'admire' - the two little words belong to the verb, not to the noun.
quests.explanation: Phrasal verbs like 'look up to' behave as a unit, so the preposition stays with the verb at the end of the clause. Forcing the preposition to the front separates the verb from its particle, and leaving out the particle changes the meaning entirely.
options: The colleague I look up to is retiring.
The colleague up to whom I look is retiring.
The colleague to whom up I look is retiring.
The colleague whom I look is retiring.
quests.correctAnswer: The colleague I look up to is retiring.

quests.question: Why is 'the plan we came up with' preferred over 'the plan up with which we came'?
quests.hint: Think about 'come up with' as a single chunk of meaning.
quests.explanation: 'Come up with' is a phrasal verb: its parts work together as one unit of meaning. Fronting only part of it splits the verb apart and sounds unnatural, so speakers keep the whole phrase in place.
options: Plans cannot be the antecedent of a relative clause.
'Come up with' works as a unit, so the whole verb phrase stays together instead of being split.
quests.correctAnswer: 'Come up with' works as a unit, so the whole verb phrase stays together instead of being split.

quests.question: The idea ___ she came up with saved the project.
quests.hint: 'Came up with' is a phrasal verb that stays together at the end of the clause. Which option can stand for 'the idea' as its object?
quests.explanation: The relative pronoun stands for 'the idea' as the object of 'came up with,' so 'that' works. 'Whom' is for people, 'in which' would add a second preposition, and 'whose' shows possession.
quests.correctAnswer: that

quests.question: She arrived at nine, ___ time the meeting had already ended.
quests.hint: The fixed phrase points back to the moment she arrived. Which preposition-and-pronoun pair fits?
quests.explanation: 'By which time' is a formal phrase meaning 'by that moment.' The preposition comes first, followed by 'which'; 'which by' reverses the order, and 'that' or 'whom' cannot follow a preposition here.
quests.correctAnswer: by which
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause

quests.question: You may submit late, in ___ case you will lose ten percent of the marks.
quests.hint: The phrase refers back to the whole idea of submitting late, not to a single noun.
quests.explanation: 'In which case' refers back to the entire situation just described. After a preposition the pronoun must be 'which'; 'that,' 'whom,' and 'what' are not possible in this fixed phrase.
quests.correctAnswer: which
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause

quests.question: He mentioned the deadline, at which point everyone panicked. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.hint: Ask what 'point' refers to - a noun in the first clause, or a moment described by the whole clause?
quests.explanation: 'At which point' refers to the moment when he mentioned the deadline - the whole event, not one noun. That is why the clause is set off by a comma.
options: The moment when he mentioned the deadline
quests.correctAnswer: The moment when he mentioned the deadline
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause

quests.question: Which version is best for a formal legal contract?
quests.hint: Formal legal writing favors fronted prepositions and complete forms rather than conversational shortcuts.
quests.explanation: The fronted preposition with 'whose' is the most formal way to express this relationship, and 'shall' fits contract language. The other versions are grammatical but conversational.
options: The party for whose benefit the trust was created shall receive the funds.
The party who the trust was created for shall receive the funds.
The party the trust was created for gets the funds.
The party that the trust was created for will get the money.
quests.correctAnswer: The party for whose benefit the trust was created shall receive the funds.

quests.question: Which sounds most natural in a text to a friend?
quests.hint: Texts are short and casual. Which version leaves the preposition at the end and drops the pronoun?
quests.explanation: In casual messages, the preposition stays at the end and the pronoun is dropped: 'the place we went to.' The fronted version sounds like a letter, and the other two repeat or misplace the preposition.
options: The place where to we went last night was packed.
The place we went to last night was packed.
The place in which we went to last night was packed.
The place to which we went last night was packed.
quests.correctAnswer: The place we went to last night was packed.

quests.question: Which sentence mixes registers awkwardly, pairing a very formal pattern with slang?
quests.hint: Look for the one where formal grammar and casual vocabulary pull in opposite directions.
quests.explanation: 'To whom' is a formal written pattern, but 'the dude' and 'super chill' are slang, so the sentence clashes. The other sentences are consistently casual or consistently formal.
options: The person to whom I spoke was extremely helpful.
The dude to whom I spoke was super chill.
The guy I spoke to was really helpful.
The person I spoke to was extremely helpful.
quests.correctAnswer: The dude to whom I spoke was super chill.

quests.question: What is the error in this sentence? 'The candidates, most of who applied online, were interviewed.'
quests.hint: Check which pronoun is allowed directly after the preposition 'of.'
quests.explanation: After a preposition, a relative pronoun for people must be 'whom' - 'most of whom.' The commas are correct because the clause is non-defining.
options: 'Who' cannot follow the preposition 'of'; 'whom' is required.
quests.correctAnswer: 'Who' cannot follow the preposition 'of'; 'whom' is required.

quests.question: What is the error in this sentence? 'The house in that we lived was demolished.'
quests.hint: Check which relative pronouns may directly follow a preposition.
quests.explanation: 'That' can never follow a preposition. The fronted pattern needs 'in which,' or the preposition can stay at the end: 'the house that we lived in.'
options: 'That' cannot follow a preposition; 'which' is required.
quests.correctAnswer: 'That' cannot follow a preposition; 'which' is required.

quests.question: Which sentence contains two separate errors?
quests.hint: Count the problems in each sentence: pronoun choice after a preposition, and comma use, are separate skills.
quests.explanation: 'The colleague to who I reported, retired last year' has two errors: 'who' cannot follow a preposition, and the comma separating subject from verb is unnecessary. The defining and non-defining versions are both correct, and the sentence with only the stray comma has one error.
options: The colleague, to whom I reported, retired last year.
The colleague to whom I reported, retired last year.
The colleague to who I reported, retired last year.
The colleague to whom I reported retired last year.
quests.correctAnswer: The colleague to who I reported, retired last year.

quests.question: The proposal from the committee, some members of which had opposed it from the start, was finally approved. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.hint: 'Members of' something - ask what group has members, and remember the comma.
quests.explanation: 'Some members of which' refers to the committee, the group that has members. 'The proposal' does not have members, and 'the start' is only a time phrase.
quests.correctAnswer: the committee

quests.question: The study surveyed forty hospitals, half of ___ nurses worked night shifts.
quests.hint: The noun 'nurses' comes right after the gap. What do the nurses belong to?
quests.explanation: 'Half of whose nurses' means 'half of those hospitals' nurses,' so the possessive 'whose' is needed. Quantifier plus 'of' plus 'whose' is a formal pattern found in reports and academic writing.
quests.correctAnswer: whose

quests.question: In 'The professor to whom I addressed the letter had already retired,' which words make up the relative clause?
quests.hint: The clause starts with the fronted preposition and ends just before the main verb.
quests.explanation: The relative clause begins with the fronted preposition 'to' and runs through 'letter.' The main verb phrase 'had already retired' belongs to 'the professor' and falls outside the clause.
options: I addressed the letter had already retired
to whom I addressed the letter
quests.correctAnswer: to whom I addressed the letter

quests.question: Which sentence is correct and suitable for a formal report?
quests.hint: Check the pronoun after 'of,' the comma before the clause, and the verb form.
quests.explanation: 'Most of whom' is the correct formal pattern for people, and the clause is non-defining, so it needs a comma before it and none after 'whom.' 'Who' and 'that' cannot follow 'of,' and dropping the comma leaves the clause unseparated.
options: The staff most of whom hold advanced degrees, were trained abroad.
The staff, most of that hold advanced degrees, were trained abroad.
The staff, most of who hold advanced degrees, were trained abroad.
The staff, most of whom hold advanced degrees, were trained abroad.
quests.correctAnswer: The staff, most of whom hold advanced degrees, were trained abroad.

quests.question: Which of these sentences is NOT acceptable in standard English?
quests.hint: Three of these are the same idea in different registers. One puts a forbidden pronoun after a preposition.
quests.explanation: 'To that' is impossible because 'that' can never follow a preposition. The other three are acceptable: pronoun dropped, fronted 'to whom,' and stranded 'whom ... to.'
options: The person I was speaking to left.
The person whom I was speaking to left.
The person to whom I was speaking left.
The person to that I was speaking left.
quests.correctAnswer: The person to that I was speaking left.

quests.question: Which statement about prepositions and relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.hint: Test each statement against what you know about fronted prepositions, quantifier clauses, and 'whose.'
quests.explanation: 'That' can never replace 'which' after a preposition, so it cannot appear in 'one of which.' The other statements are true: quantifier clauses are non-defining, people take 'whom' after a preposition, and 'whose' can follow one.
options: 'Whose' can follow a preposition, as in 'on whose behalf.'
In a quantifier clause such as 'one of which,' the word 'that' can replace 'which.'
After a preposition, a relative pronoun for a person must be 'whom.'
'Most of whom' and 'all of which' introduce non-defining clauses.
quests.correctAnswer: In a quantifier clause such as 'one of which,' the word 'that' can replace 'which.'
